content_voiceover: This is a British Journal of Cancer paper from a Taiwan multicenter study comparing children and adults with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with front-line imatinib. The key finding is that children have a slower molecular response than adults, even though their overall survival is comparable. The graph plots the international scale percentage of BCR-ABL1 transcript, on a log scale, against years of imatinib therapy, comparing children in black to adults in gray. Both groups start at essentially 100 percent transcript level before treatment. As therapy continues, both groups decline, but the adult curve drops faster and stays consistently lower than the children's curve at every time point from 3 months out through 13 years. The table underneath gives the median international scale percentage at each time point along with the ratio of children to adults, which is greater than 1 throughout, meaning children retain relatively more residual disease at the same time point compared to adults. This has practical implications for boards, because it means the molecular milestones you use to judge treatment response, like achieving a major molecular response by certain time points, may need to be interpreted with more patience in pediatric patients, since slower response does not necessarily mean treatment failure or the need to switch tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
keypoints: Taiwan multicenter study found children with CML on front-line imatinib have slower molecular response than adults
Children versus adults ratio of median international scale percentage remains greater than 1 at every timepoint measured
Despite slower response kinetics, overall survival in children was comparable to adults
Clinical implication is that slower molecular response in pediatric CML should not be misread as treatment failure
keypoint_voiceover: Key testable point is that pediatric CML patients on imatinib achieve molecular responses more slowly than adults, as shown by a persistently higher BCR-ABL1 transcript level at every timepoint. However, this slower kinetics does not translate into worse survival, so clinicians should be cautious before switching tyrosine kinase inhibitors based on response timing alone in children.
